summary.title: When AI builds itself
summary.one_liner: Anthropic's Institute argues AI is already speeding up AI development, presents internal and public evidence on recursive self-improvement, and sketches three possible futures.
keywords: anthropic internal data on ai productivity
takeaways: Anthropic reports that over 80% of merged code as of May 2026 was authored by Claude, and that engineers merge about 8x as much code per day as in 2024 (noting lines of code is an imperfect measure).
Public benchmarks show task-length capability doubling roughly every four months, and SWE-bench and CORE-Bench saturating within about two years and fifteen months respectively.

Claude is now strong at well-specified experiments (about 52x speedup on a training-code optimization task vs about 4x for a skilled human in 4-8 hours), but still lags in choosing goals and research taste, where it beat human next-step choices 64% of the time in one study.

The article describes three scenarios: a stalled trend, AI labs with compounding efficiency gains and humans setting direction, and full recursive self-improvement with humans shifting to oversight and verification.
Anthropic flags Amdahl's law: speeding up one step shifts the bottleneck, and human code review is already one such bottleneck.
summary.summary: The Anthropic Institute essay argues that AI is already accelerating AI development and that full recursive self-improvement, where AI designs its own successor, could arrive sooner than institutions expect. It combines public benchmark trends (METR task length, SWE-bench, CORE-Bench) with internal Anthropic data on code authorship, output per engineer, bug review, and experiment-running performance. It also reports a few small studies, such as agents running an open AI safety research task and a comparison of Claude's and humans' next-step choices in research sessions, with stated caveats. The piece closes by outlining three future scenarios and the risks each carries, including loss of control.
